unit-1.title: All About Me and My Family
unit-1.description: Challenge 1 of Stage 1: Families, friends, community and culture.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 -- Asking Questions About Our Families
lessons.objectives: Think of simple questions to find out about family life; begin to gather information by asking others.

steps.title: Asking questions to find out
steps.definition: Asking a question is how we find out things we don't already know.
steps.example: If I want to know what a friend's family likes to eat together, I could ask: "What food does your family enjoy?"

cards.label: Who?
cards.content: Asks about a person. "Who lives in your house?"

cards.label: What?
cards.content: Asks about a thing. "What do you do together on weekends?"

cards.label: Where?
cards.content: Asks about a place. "Where does your family like to visit?"

cards.question: You want to know how many people are in your friend's family. What could you ask?
cards.answer: "Who is in your family?" or "How many people live in your house?"

cards.question: You want to know what your friend's family does for fun. What could you ask?
cards.answer: "What does your family like to do together?"

summaryPoints: Asking a question is how we find out things we don't already know.
Who, what and where are useful question words.
homeworkItems: Ask a family member one "who", "what" or "where" question and remember their answer.

teachingScript.overview: Model asking a real question to one child in front of the class before children practise in pairs -- seeing a live example makes the skill concrete.

talkingPoints: Ask one child a real question about their family and show how the answer gives you new information.
Practise each question word chorally, then have children suggest their own example question for each.
Let children attempt their own question aloud before revealing the suggested one -- there's more than one right answer here.
Pair children up for one minute to practise asking each other a real question.

quizQuestions.question: Asking a question helps us to...
options: Find out something we don't already know
Tell someone what we already know

quizQuestions.question: Which question word would you use to ask about a place?

flashcards.definition: Something we ask to find out information we don't already know.
A question word used to ask about a person.
A question word used to ask about a thing.
A question word used to ask about a place.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Asking Questions About Our Families
worksheetContent.instructions: Ask a family member these questions and write or draw their answers.

questions.prompt: Ask: "Who is in our family?" Draw everyone you find out about.
Ask: "What do we like to do together?" Draw or write the answer.
Think of one more question you could ask about your family.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 -- Same and Different Families
lessons.objectives: Look at information about different families and notice things that are the same and things that are different; share a simple opinion.

steps.title: Same and different
steps.definition: When we look closely at information, we can notice things that are the same between people, and things that are different.
steps.example: Two families might both enjoy eating together (the same), but one family might have grandparents living with them and another might not (different).

cards.definition: Some families are small, some are big -- and both are wonderful.

cards.term: What language do you speak at home?
cards.definition: Some families speak one language, some speak more than one.
Favourite family foods can be very different from house to house.

items.label: A family with grandparents living in the same house.
items.reason: Only sort this here if your own family doesn't have grandparents at home -- otherwise it goes in "Same as mine"! There's no single right answer -- it depends on your own family.

items.label: A family that eats dinner together every night.
items.reason: Many families eat together, but the important skill here is comparing to your OWN family honestly, not guessing what's "correct".

items.label: A family that speaks two languages at home.
items.reason: Again -- sort based on your own real family, not a fixed answer.

items.label: A family that celebrates a festival together.
items.reason: Compare honestly to your own family's celebrations.

summaryPoints: Every family has things that are the same as others, and things that are different.
There is no "correct" kind of family -- all families are different and all are valued.
homeworkItems: Ask a family member one thing they think makes your family special or different.

teachingScript.overview: This lesson is deliberately open-ended -- the sorting activity has no single correct answer, since it depends on each child's own real family. Emphasise there is no "right" kind of family throughout.

talkingPoints: Use two real, contrasting examples from the class (with permission) to show a genuine same/different comparison.
Invite a few children to share their own answer to each fact before revealing the card's note.
Make explicit that children sort based on THEIR OWN family, not a guessed "correct" answer -- this is about honest comparison, not getting it right.
misconceptions: Children may worry there's a "correct" family type to compare against -- reassure repeatedly that all family types are valid and normal.

talkingPoints: Close by naming one thing that's the same across every family in the room (e.g. everyone has people who care about them).

quizQuestions.question: When we compare two families, we might notice...
options: Only things that are the same
Things that are the same AND things that are different

quizQuestions.question: Is there one "correct" kind of family?
options: Yes, only one kind is correct
No -- all families are different, and all are valued

flashcards.definition: Things that are alike between two people or families.
Things that are not alike between two people or families.
To look at two things and notice what's the same and what's different.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Same and Different Families
worksheetContent.instructions: Think about your own family for these questions.

questions.prompt: Draw one thing about your family that you think might be the same as a friend's family.
Draw one thing about your family that might be different from a friend's family.
Tell a grown-up: why is it good that families can be different from each other?

lessons.title: Lesson 3 -- Working Together and Listening to Others
lessons.objectives: Work with a partner or small group to share information; listen to someone else's idea, even when it is different from your own.

steps.title: Working together
steps.definition: Working together means sharing ideas with a partner and listening carefully to their ideas too, even when they are different from your own.
steps.example: If you think your family's favourite food is rice and your partner says theirs is noodles, working together means listening to both ideas, not only sharing your own.

cards.label: Share your idea
cards.content: Tell your partner what you think, in a clear voice.

cards.label: Listen to their idea
cards.content: Wait quietly and really listen while your partner shares.

cards.label: Different ideas are okay
cards.content: Your partner's idea can be different from yours, and that's completely fine.

cards.question: Your partner shares an idea you don't agree with, so you say "that's wrong" and ignore them. Is this good teamwork?
cards.answer: No -- a better response is to listen fully, then share your own idea too. Both ideas can be shared.

cards.question: You listen to your partner's idea, then say "that's interesting, I thought something different too" and share yours. Is this good teamwork?
cards.answer: Yes! You listened first, then shared your own idea kindly.

summaryPoints: Working together means sharing your own idea AND listening to your partner's idea.
Different ideas are okay -- we don't need to agree on everything.
homeworkItems: Practise listening carefully while a family member talks, without interrupting.

teachingScript.overview: Pair children up for a short real task (comparing family facts from Lesson 1/2) so the collaboration skill is practised on genuine content, not a hypothetical.

talkingPoints: Role-play a bad example (talking over your partner) and a good example (listening then sharing) live.
Ask children to demonstrate "listening posture" (facing your partner, quiet body) before practising.
Let children spot what's wrong with the bad example in their own words before revealing the answer.
Pair children up to share one family fact each and practise listening to their partner's fact too.
misconceptions: Children at this age often want to talk at the same time as their partner -- gently remind them of the talking-piece idea from English lessons if useful.

quizQuestions.question: Working together means...
options: Sharing your idea AND listening to others' ideas

quizQuestions.question: If your partner has a different idea from you, you should...
options: Say they're wrong and ignore them
Listen to their idea, then share your own too

flashcards.definition: Working together with someone, sharing ideas and listening to theirs too.
Working well together with a partner or group.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Working Together and Listening to Others
worksheetContent.instructions: Do this worksheet with a partner if possible.

questions.prompt: Draw yourself sharing an idea with a partner.
Draw yourself listening to your partner's idea.
Tell a grown-up one idea your partner shared that was different from your own.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 -- Sharing What We Found Out
lessons.objectives: Present something learned about family and community to the class using pictures or simple words; say what was interesting about what was learned.

steps.title: Sharing what we found out
steps.definition: Presenting means telling other people what you found out, using pictures, objects, or simple words.
steps.example: You could hold up your family drawing and say: "I found out that my family likes to cook together on weekends."

cards.label: Clear voice
cards.content: Speak loud and clear so everyone listening can hear you.

cards.label: Show your picture
cards.content: Hold up your drawing or picture so everyone can see it too.

cards.label: Say one clear fact
cards.content: Share one thing you found out -- you don't need to say everything at once.

summaryPoints: Presenting means telling others what we found out, using pictures or words.
A clear voice, showing your picture, and sharing one fact make a good presentation.
homeworkItems: Practise saying your one family fact out loud at home before presenting it to the class.

teachingScript.overview: This is a sharing/presenting lesson -- most of the time should be spent on children actually presenting their family drawings from earlier lessons to a partner or small group, not more input.

talkingPoints: Model presenting your own "family fact" example first, using the three tips explicitly.
Have children practise just the "clear voice" tip alone first with a partner before combining all three.
Give as much time as possible for children to actually present their own family fact/drawing to a partner or small group -- this is the heart of the lesson.
misconceptions: Shy children may want to skip presenting altogether -- offer presenting to just one partner as a gentler first step rather than the whole class.

quizQuestions.question: When presenting, it helps to...
options: Speak clearly and show your picture

quizQuestions.question: A good presentation shares...
options: Every single detail you know, very fast
One clear fact, in a clear voice

flashcards.definition: Telling other people what you found out, using pictures, objects or words.
A true piece of information you found out.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Sharing What We Found Out
worksheetContent.instructions: Use your family drawing from earlier lessons to help you present.

questions.prompt: Write or draw the one fact about your family you will share with the class.
Practise saying your fact out loud three times.
After presenting, draw a smiley face if you felt proud of sharing!

unit-2.title: Looking After Our Environment
unit-2.description: Challenge 2 of Stage 1: Looking after planet Earth.

lessons.title: Lesson 5 -- Asking Questions About Our Environment
lessons.objectives: Think of simple questions about the natural environment around us; begin to gather information by looking closely and asking others.

steps.title: Asking questions about our environment
steps.definition: Our environment is everything around us in nature -- the beach, the sea, the trees, the animals. We can ask questions to find out more about it.
steps.example: Walking near the beach, you might ask: "What lives in the sea near us?" or "Why is there rubbish on the sand?"

cards.label: What lives here?
cards.content: Asks about the plants and animals in a place, like fish in the sea.

cards.label: What has changed?
cards.content: Asks whether a place looks different than it used to.

cards.label: Why does this happen?
cards.content: Asks the reason behind something we notice, like why rubbish washes up on the beach.

cards.question: You notice plastic bags on the beach. What question could you ask?
cards.answer: "Why is there plastic on the beach?" or "Where does this rubbish come from?"

cards.question: You see lots of small crabs near the rocks. What question could you ask?
cards.answer: "What do the crabs eat?" or "Where do the crabs live?"

summaryPoints: Our environment is everything around us in nature.
We can ask questions like what lives here, what has changed, and why something happens.
homeworkItems: Look closely at one part of nature near your home (a garden, the beach, a tree) and think of one question about it.

teachingScript.overview: If possible, take the class outside or to a window looking at nature before asking children to generate their own questions -- real observation grounds the skill.

talkingPoints: Look outside together (or at a photo of the local beach) and ask what children notice before modelling a question.
Connect each question type back to something visible near the school if possible.
Accept multiple valid questions from children, not just the one given as the answer.
Have each child name one thing in nature they'd like to know more about.

quizQuestions.question: "Why is there rubbish on the beach?" is an example of a...

flashcards.definition: Everything around us in nature -- the beach, the sea, the trees, the animals.
To see and pay attention to something.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Asking Questions About Our Environment
worksheetContent.instructions: Look closely at nature near your home before answering.

questions.prompt: Draw one plant or animal you see near your home.
Write or say one question you have about it.
Ask a grown-up your question. What did they say?

lessons.title: Lesson 6 -- What Helps and What Harms Our Environment
lessons.objectives: Look at information about human actions and sort them into ones that help and ones that harm the environment; share a simple opinion.

steps.title: Helping and harming our environment
steps.definition: Some things people do help our environment stay healthy, and some things harm it.
steps.example: Planting a tree helps the environment. Dropping plastic on the beach harms it.

cards.definition: Helps -- trees give animals a home and clean the air.
Harms -- animals can get hurt and the beach becomes dirty.
Helps -- it keeps the beach clean and safe for animals.

items.label: Putting plastic bottles in a recycling bin.
items.reason: Recycling means the plastic can be reused instead of becoming rubbish in nature.

items.label: Throwing a plastic bag onto the sand.
items.reason: Litter can hurt animals and pollutes the beach.

items.label: Watering a young plant so it can grow.
items.reason: Caring for plants helps them grow and support other living things.

items.label: Burning rubbish in an open pile.
items.reason: Burning rubbish can pollute the air that people and animals breathe.

summaryPoints: Some actions help our environment, like planting trees and recycling.
Some actions harm our environment, like littering and burning rubbish.
homeworkItems: Notice one action at home that helps the environment and tell your class tomorrow.

teachingScript.overview: Use real, local examples throughout (the beach, plastic waste, planting) so the helps/harms distinction connects to the children's actual surroundings.

talkingPoints: Show two real or pictured examples (a clean beach and a littered one) and ask children which they'd rather visit, before naming help/harm.
Ask children to guess whether each action helps or harms before flipping the card.
Encourage children to explain WHY each action helps or harms, not just sort it correctly.
misconceptions: Children may think an action is automatically "harmful" just because it involves something they dislike (e.g. bugs) -- keep the focus on real environmental impact.

talkingPoints: Ask children to share one helping action they could try themselves this week.

quizQuestions.question: Planting a tree is an action that...
Throwing a plastic bag onto the sand is an action that...

flashcards.definition: An action that is good for our environment, like planting a tree.
An action that is bad for our environment, like littering.
Reusing materials like plastic instead of throwing them away.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- What Helps and What Harms Our Environment
worksheetContent.instructions: Think about actions you have seen at home, at school, or at the beach.

questions.prompt: Draw one action that helps the environment.
Draw one action that harms the environment.
Tell a grown-up: which helping action could YOU do this week?

lessons.title: Lesson 7 -- Working Together to Help Our Environment
lessons.objectives: Work with a partner or small group to plan one simple action that helps the environment; listen to and combine different ideas.

steps.title: Planning together
steps.definition: When we plan together, everyone shares an idea, and the group picks or combines ideas to make one plan.
steps.example: One person suggests picking up litter, another suggests planting seeds -- the group might decide to do both!

cards.label: Everyone shares an idea
cards.content: Each person in the group says one idea for helping the environment.

cards.label: Listen to every idea
cards.content: The group listens carefully to all the ideas before choosing.

cards.label: Pick or combine a plan
cards.content: The group agrees on one plan, using one idea or mixing a few together.

cards.question: One person in the group only wants to do their own idea and won't listen to anyone else's. Is this good group planning?
cards.answer: No -- good planning means listening to everyone's ideas, not just your own.

cards.question: The group listens to three ideas, then agrees to try two of them together. Is this good group planning?
cards.answer: Yes! Everyone was heard, and the group combined good ideas.

summaryPoints: Planning together means everyone shares an idea and the group listens to all of them.
A group can pick one idea or combine a few together.
homeworkItems: Tell a family member the plan your group agreed on to help the environment.

teachingScript.overview: Put children into small groups of 3-4 to actually plan one real, doable class environmental action (a litter pick, planting seeds, a poster) -- the planning should lead to a genuine follow-up activity.

talkingPoints: Give a quick real example of the class combining two ideas for something else earlier in the term, if one exists, to ground the concept.
Physically go through the three steps as a whole-class example planning one shared action, before splitting into small groups.
Role-play the "won't listen" example briefly so the contrast is vivid.
Give small groups 10 minutes to plan one real class environmental action, then have each group share their plan in one sentence.
misconceptions: In small groups, one confident child may dominate the plan -- circulate and prompt quieter children to share their idea directly.

quizQuestions.question: Good group planning means...
options: Everyone shares an idea and the group listens to all of them

quizQuestions.question: A group can turn several ideas into one plan by...

flashcards.definition: A decision about what to do, made after sharing and listening to ideas.
To put two or more ideas together.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Working Together to Help Our Environment
worksheetContent.instructions: Think about the plan your group made in class.

questions.prompt: Draw the environmental action your group planned.
Write or say whose idea helped make the plan.
Tell a grown-up when your group will try the plan.

lessons.title: Lesson 8 -- Sharing Our Ideas to Help the Planet
lessons.objectives: Present the group's environmental action plan to the class; reflect on what was learned across the Challenge and say what surprised or interested them.

steps.title: Thinking back on what we learned
steps.definition: Reflecting means thinking back over everything we learned and saying what was interesting, surprising, or important to us.
steps.example: You might say: "I was surprised that even small rubbish can hurt sea animals -- that's why I want to help pick up litter."

cards.label: "I learned that..."
cards.content: Used to share a new fact you found out.

cards.label: "I was surprised that..."
cards.content: Used to share something you didn't expect.

cards.label: "Now I want to..."
cards.content: Used to share an action you'd like to try because of what you learned.

summaryPoints: Reflecting means thinking back and sharing what was interesting, surprising, or important.
Our group plans are one way we turn what we learned into real action.
homeworkItems: Try your group's environmental action plan at home or with your family, if you can.

teachingScript.overview: Most of this lesson should be groups presenting their environmental plan from Lesson 7, followed by a short whole-class reflection using the sentence starters.

talkingPoints: Model your own reflection sentence about something you learned from the class this week.
Have children practise each sentence starter with a partner before presenting to the whole class.
Give each group 1-2 minutes to present their environmental plan, then invite two or three children to share a reflection sentence.
misconceptions: Groups may want to only describe WHAT they'll do, not WHY -- gently prompt them to add one reason.

quizQuestions.question: Reflecting means...
options: Thinking back and sharing what was interesting or important

quizQuestions.question: "I was surprised that..." is a sentence starter used for...
options: Sharing something unexpected that you learned

flashcards.definition: To think back over what we learned and share what was interesting or important.
Feeling like something happened that you didn't expect.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Sharing Our Ideas to Help the Planet
worksheetContent.instructions: Think back over everything we learned in this Challenge.

questions.prompt: Finish this sentence: "I learned that..."
Finish this sentence: "I was surprised that..."
Finish this sentence: "Now I want to..."
